lines.text: Tonight, at exactly midnight, the Moon disappears.
No explosion. No warning. It's just... gone.
And for one strange second, nobody on Earth notices.
Moonlight takes about one point three seconds to reach us. So the last light the Moon ever reflected is still on its way.
The full Moon is the brightest thing in the night sky. Now, every night is a moonless night. Only the stars are left.
Out on the reefs, many corals use moonlight as a clock, to know when to spawn. Tonight, that clock stops.
By morning, the oceans start to feel it.
The Moon is the main reason we have tides. The Sun pulls on the oceans too, but with less than half the strength.
So the tides don't vanish. They shrink. High tide gets lower. Low tide gets higher.
Tide pools, crabs, snails, the birds that feed at the water's edge. Their whole world just got smaller.
And that's only the first morning.
Because the Moon wasn't just lighting our nights. It was holding our planet steady. And without it, Earth's tilt could start to wander.
